newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egypt stems flow of foreign funds to t-bills.
newsitem.headline: Egypt stems flow of foreign funds to t-bills.

text.p: Cairo bankers said on Tuesday the central bank gave local banks preference over non-residents in Monday's auction of 182-day t-bills, in effect stemming the flow of foreign funds into the market.
The bank rejected some bids from non-residents, even though they fell within the range of bids accepted, they said.
The move, a deviation from previous central bank practice, brought the Egyptian pound down a fraction and pushed up Egyptian pound interbank rates, the bankers said.

Bankers quoted the dollar at between 3.3880 and 3.3920 pounds bid and between 3.3890 and 3.3960 offered. Overnight interbank rates rose to between 9-1/2 and 10 percent, from between 8-1/2 and 9-1/4 percent on Monday, they added.
A Central Bank official declined to confirm or deny the bank had rejected such bids, saying he would need details of specific bids by non-resident institutions.
"They are restricting the amount of t-bills they give to non-residents. They fear they have lost control of the short end of the yield curve," one banker said.
"If non-residents go on buying, interbank rates will fall below nine percent and they don't want that now," he added.

Foreign investors have accounted for a substantial amount of the money invested in the Egyptian t-bill market but the strong demand for the bills has made the Egyptian pound appreciate and brought down pound interbank rates.
It was not clear whether the selective approach to foreign bids was a one-off response to the market or the central bank would do the same at Wednesday's auction of 91-day bills.
One banker said he could detect no system in the way the central bank handled t-bill bids from non-residents on Monday. "There were no rules," he said.

The bankers said the change of tack by the central bank brough the Egyptian pound down because less dollars came into the market and non-residents whose t-bills matured on Tuesday could not roll them over into new bills.

One banker speculated that by accepting a higher proportion of bids from local banks the central bank aimed to tighten Egyptian pound liquidity and hold up the interbank rates, which in recent weeks have fallen to levels unknown for several years.

Egyptian t-bills are an attractive instrument for non-residents because of the relatively high yield -- an average of 9.921 percent in Monday's auction -- without any appreciable risk of devaluation against the dollar.
But the inflow of foreign funds into Egypt does have some undesireable side effects. The Central Bank has to buy up all the foreign currency to stop the pound appreciating.
